newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Albert Fisher shares slip as talks halted.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Albert Fisher shares slip as talks halted.

text.p: British food processing and distribution company Albert Fisher Group Plc disappointed the stockmarket on Thursday by announcing it had terminated talks to sell the company.
"In the board's opinion, the potential offeror was not in a position to make an offer which could be recommended to shareholders," the company said in a statement.
Although Fisher did not reveal the identity of the bidder, market rumours have centred increasingly on American banana supplier Chiquita Brands.

Instead, Fisher said, the group would split itself up and offer parts of the business for sale, possibly enabling it to buy back some of its own shares. The group said it would put proposals for a share buyback to shareholders as soon as possible.
The group's shares fell 6-1/2p to 37p, having hit 35p in early trading on Thursday, as gloom set in among shareholders.

"A lot of people will be disappointed with this news. The company has now got to try and realise value by selling businesses off, and that will mean a lot more uncertainty, not least over the cost of divestments and the timescale over which those divestments will take place," said Carl Short, an analyst at SocGen.

The group has some 30 subsidiaries, ranging widely from cockle processor Roem van Yerseke off the Dutch coast and prawn processor Morubel in Belgium to supplying salads to supermarket chains and sauces to fast food chain McDonalds.

Fisher is divided into four divisions, European fresh produce, which includes Saphir Fruit, European food processing, a Seafood unit in Britain and Holland, which include MacFish and Forman Fish both based in Scotland, and a fresh fruit and vegetables business in North America called River Ranch.

"It's disappointing, the long suffering shareholders have been waiting with their hands together for this bid to materialise. Clearly no bid is bad news which is why the share price has reacted," said one analyst who chose not to be named.

The company has not announced a dividend increase for several years and its earnings have continued to suffer from the vagaries of weather and crop pricing. The company announced a 1.6 percent increase to 19.1 million pounds ($30.3 million) in its pretax profit for the six months to February 28, 1997 and held its dividend at 1.85 pence per share.

In July Fisher said it was in talks with an undisclosed party and analysts predicted at the time it was more likely to fall prey to a venture capital firm looking at its break up value rather than another food company.
Analysts estimates of the group's break up value range from about 48 pence per share equivalent to about 445 million pound excluding debt, to 480 million.

Albert Fisher said results for the year to August 31 should be broadly in line with last year, despite pressure from sterling's strength. The company also planned to pay an unchanged final dividend for the year.
Last year, the company posted pretax profits of 40.1 million pounds on turnover of 1.24 billion, with a final dividend of 1.90p per share. ($ = 0.630 British Pounds)
